questions.explanation: 'Despite' and 'in spite of' are followed by a noun or -ing form: Despite the cold, we swam.

wrongReasons.although: 'although' must be followed by a clause, not a noun phrase.
wrongReasons.however: 'however' links two sentences; it cannot introduce a noun phrase like this.

questions.text: ___ the heavy rain, the outdoor concert went ahead as planned.

questions.explanation: 'So + adjective + that' expresses result: It was so hot that we stayed in.

wrongReasons.such: 'such' is used before a noun phrase, e.g. 'such a fierce storm'.

questions.text: The storm was ___ fierce that the ferry crossing was cancelled.

questions.explanation: 'So that' expresses purpose and is followed by a clause: I left early so that I could rest.

wrongReasons.in order: 'in order' is followed by 'to', not 'that', in modern English.
wrongReasons.such: 'such that' expresses result or degree, not purpose.

questions.text: She took a taxi ___ that she wouldn't miss the start of the show.

questions.explanation: 'In case' means 'as a precaution because something might happen'.

wrongReasons.if: 'in if' is not possible; the linker is 'in case'.

questions.text: I will leave a spare key with the neighbours in ___ you get home before me.

questions.explanation: 'Even though' adds emphasis to a contrast: Even though it was late, she called.

wrongReasons.although: 'although though' is impossible; only 'even' combines with 'though'.
wrongReasons.despite: 'despite' is not used with 'though' and cannot introduce a clause.

questions.text: ___ though he had trained for months, he failed to finish the race.

questions.explanation: 'As far as ... is concerned' limits a statement to one area: As far as I'm concerned, it's fine.

wrongReasons.long: 'as long as' means 'provided that', not 'with regard to'.
wrongReasons.much: 'as much as' compares quantity and does not fit 'concerned'.

questions.text: The film was a success as ___ as the critics were concerned, but it lost money.

questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by an -ing form: Despite knowing the risks, she went.

wrongReasons.although: 'although' needs a full clause with a subject and finite verb.
wrongReasons.even though: 'even though' is followed by a clause, not by an -ing form.

questions.text: ___ having a degree in law, he has never worked as a lawyer.

questions.explanation: 'Provided (that)' and 'on condition that' introduce a condition: You can go provided that you call.

wrongReasons.unless: 'unless that' is not possible, and 'unless' means 'if not'.
wrongReasons.in case: 'in case that' is not used and expresses precaution, not condition.

questions.text: You may borrow the equipment ___ that it is returned by Monday.

questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not': Unless you hurry, you'll be late.

wrongReasons.if: 'If we leave now, we'll miss it' is illogical; we need 'unless'.
wrongReasons.provided: 'provided' introduces a positive condition, which makes no sense here.

questions.text: ___ we leave now, we'll miss the last train.

questions.explanation: A comma + 'which' can refer to a whole previous clause: He was late, which annoyed us.

wrongReasons.that: 'that' cannot be used after a comma to refer back to a whole clause.
wrongReasons.what: 'what' means 'the thing that' and cannot refer back to a clause.

questions.text: The factory closed, ___ resulted in hundreds of job losses.

questions.explanation: 'Contrary to' introduces an idea that is not true: Contrary to expectations, he won.

wrongReasons.opposite: 'Opposite to popular belief' is not the fixed phrase.
wrongReasons.contrast: We say 'in contrast to', not 'contrast to'.

questions.text: ___ to popular belief, bats are not actually blind.

questions.explanation: 'Due to' and 'owing to' are followed by a noun phrase and give a reason.

wrongReasons.result: 'result to' is not correct; we say 'as a result of'.

questions.text: The festival was cancelled ___ to a lack of funding.

questions.explanation: 'Hardly ever' means 'almost never': I hardly ever eat out.

wrongReasons.almost: We say 'almost never' but not 'almost ever'.
wrongReasons.nearly: 'nearly ever' is not correct; use 'hardly ever'.

questions.text: I ___ ever go to the cinema these days; I watch films at home instead.

questions.explanation: 'Almost' and 'virtually' mean 'very nearly' and work with absolute adjectives like 'identical'.

wrongReasons.hardly: 'hardly identical' means 'very different', which contradicts the sentence.
wrongReasons.most: 'most' does not modify adjectives like this; we need 'almost'.

questions.text: The two reports were ___ identical; only the dates differed.

questions.explanation: 'Already' in questions shows surprise that something happened sooner than expected.

wrongReasons.yet: 'yet' goes at the end of a question, not before the main verb.
wrongReasons.still: 'still' shows something continues, so it does not fit 'finished'.

questions.text: Have you ___ finished? That was quick!

questions.explanation: 'Still' before a negative auxiliary stresses that something expected has not happened.

wrongReasons.yet: 'yet' goes at the end of a negative sentence: 'haven't heard back yet'.
wrongReasons.already: 'already' is not used before a negative auxiliary like this.

questions.text: I ___ haven't heard back from the bank, even though I wrote to them a month ago.

questions.explanation: Extreme adjectives like 'breathtaking' take 'absolutely' or 'utterly', not 'very'.

wrongReasons.very: 'very' is not used with extreme adjectives such as 'breathtaking'.
wrongReasons.fairly: 'fairly' weakens the adjective and does not combine with extreme adjectives.

questions.text: The view from the summit was ___ breathtaking.

questions.explanation: 'Fully aware' and 'well aware' are common collocations meaning 'completely aware'.

wrongReasons.highly: 'highly' collocates with words like 'likely' or 'successful', not 'aware'.

questions.text: Before signing, she was ___ aware of the risks involved.

questions.explanation: 'Just in time' means at the last moment before it was too late.

wrongReasons.nearly: 'nearly in time' suggests we failed, which contradicts 'to catch'.
wrongReasons.hardly: 'hardly in time' is not idiomatic; we say 'only just in time'.

questions.text: We reached the platform ___ in time to catch the last train.

questions.explanation: Negative adverbs like 'rarely' at the start cause inversion: Rarely do we see her.

wrongReasons.often: 'Often' is not negative, so it does not cause inversion.
wrongReasons.sometimes: 'Sometimes' does not cause inversion of subject and auxiliary.

questions.text: ___ do we get the chance to see such rare birds in this area.

questions.explanation: 'Hard' is both an adjective and an adverb meaning 'with effort': He trains hard.

wrongReasons.hardly: 'hardly' means 'almost not', the opposite of what is meant.
wrongReasons.hardy: 'hardy' is an adjective meaning 'strong', not an adverb.

questions.text: She works ___; she's always the first to arrive and the last to leave.

questions.explanation: Before a past participle we use the adverb 'wrongly': The letter was wrongly delivered.

wrongReasons.wrong: Before a participle the adverb form 'wrongly' is required.
wrongReasons.bad: 'bad' is an adjective and cannot modify 'addressed'.

questions.text: The parcel was ___ addressed, so it was returned to the sender.

questions.explanation: To describe how someone speaks we use an adverb: She spoke quietly.

wrongReasons.quiet: 'quiet' is an adjective; after 'spoke' we need 'quietly'.
wrongReasons.loudly: 'loudly' contradicts the fact that nobody could hear him.

questions.text: He spoke so ___ that nobody at the back of the hall could hear him.

questions.explanation: 'Consequently' and 'as a result' introduce a result: It rained; consequently, we stayed in.

wrongReasons.however: 'however' introduces a contrast, not a result.
wrongReasons.nevertheless: 'nevertheless' means 'despite this', which does not fit a result.

questions.text: The bus was late, and ___ I missed my connection.

questions.explanation: Adverbs like 'definitely' come before 'not' to strengthen it: I'm definitely not going.

wrongReasons.definite: 'definite' is an adjective; we need the adverb 'definitely'.
wrongReasons.certain: 'certain' is an adjective and cannot modify 'not going'.

questions.text: I'm ___ not going to lend him money again after last time.

questions.explanation: 'Early' forms its comparative with -er: earlier, not 'more early'.

wrongReasons.more early: 'early' is a short word, so its comparative is 'earlier'.
wrongReasons.early: After 'much' and before 'than' we need the comparative form.

questions.text: The meeting finished much ___ than expected, so we all went for coffee.

questions.explanation: Comparatives are intensified with 'much', 'far' or 'a lot', not 'very': much better.

wrongReasons.more: 'more better' is a double comparative and is incorrect.

questions.text: She sings ___ better than her sister.

questions.explanation: 'Too' means more than is acceptable: It's too cold to swim.

wrongReasons.very: 'very' does not show that the speed was excessive for the conditions.
wrongReasons.enough: 'enough' goes after adjectives and adverbs, e.g. 'fast enough'.

questions.text: He was driving ___ fast for the icy conditions and skidded off the road.

questions.explanation: 'Hardly' and 'barely' mean 'almost not' and come before the adjective: It's hardly fair.

wrongReasons.no: 'no' cannot negate an adjective like 'clear' here; use 'not'.
wrongReasons.none: 'none' is a pronoun and cannot modify an adjective.

questions.text: The instructions were ___ clear enough for a beginner to follow.

questions.explanation: Sentence adverbs like 'fortunately' comment on the whole sentence and are followed by a comma.

wrongReasons.fortunate: 'fortunate' is an adjective; a sentence comment needs the adverb.

questions.text: ___, all the passengers were unhurt when the train came off the rails.

questions.explanation: Superlatives are intensified with 'by far', 'easily' or 'arguably': She is by far the fastest.

wrongReasons.very: 'very the best' is wrong; 'very' goes after 'the': 'the very best'.
